title: A dependable supply of transplantable animal hearts

concept.text: The innovation would be a dependable supply of animal hearts that can replace failing human hearts and sustain recipients for years with acceptable safety, function and quality of life. The approach represented in the supplied evidence uses genetically modified pig hearts, with genetic changes intended to improve acceptance and compatibility in humans and control organ growth. Achieving the concept requires both durable clinical performance and a practical system for producing, screening and delivering suitable donor hearts.

Conceptual synthesis: the defining capability is repeatable cardiac replacement supported by a reliable organ supply. A successful operation or several weeks of graft function establishes only part of that capability. The full innovation would connect donor-animal production, organ quality, transplantation, recipient treatment and long-term surveillance into a reproducible clinical service.

significance.text: If animal hearts could be supplied reproducibly and deliver durable outcomes comparable to human donor hearts, transplantation could become substantially less constrained by human donor availability. That would address a central limitation on cardiac replacement: obtaining a suitable living organ. The sponsor identifies expansion of transplantable-organ supply as a goal, but the supplied evidence does not demonstrate that this supply or the required long-term outcomes have been achieved.

Conditional downstream synthesis: a more predictable organ supply could make transplantation available to more eligible patients and allow more planned treatment pathways. These benefits would depend on donor-heart quality, delivery capacity, clinical eligibility, recipient outcomes and feasible resource requirements. Producing more organs alone would not establish broad access or eliminate the burdens of transplantation and ongoing treatment.

Lessons from heart xenotransplantation might inform other organ programs through compatibility engineering, immunomodulation and pathogen surveillance. That possibility should remain conditional: successful cardiac transplantation would not establish the safety or efficacy of animal kidneys, livers or lungs. Each organ program would need its own evidence, and the short-term human heart function reported here does not establish the durable performance required for the proposed transformation.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central unsolved capability is durable compatibility between an animal heart and a human recipient. The clinical report identifies antibody-mediated rejection as an obstacle requiring further advances. Genetic modification and immunomodulatory treatment must protect the graft sufficiently for sustained function while keeping the harms of treatment acceptable. Initial acceptance and good pumping function over several weeks do not establish that this balance can persist for years.

Compatibility also encompasses coagulation, physiological function and organ growth. The sponsor describes genetic edits intended to improve acceptance, compatibility and growth, and plans to monitor arrhythmias, thromboembolic events and ischemic strokes. These support the importance of managing those risks, but the supplied material does not establish their precise mechanisms, relative contribution to graft failure or whether the proposed engineering resolves them.

Infectious safety remains a separate requirement. The clinical report describes pathogen screening and immunomodulation, while the planned study includes opportunistic infections, animal-to-human infections and lifelong zoonotic surveillance. A workable approach must therefore address both infections associated with recipient treatment and possible transmission from the animal donor. Screening and monitoring are necessary safeguards; their inclusion in a protocol does not demonstrate that the residual risks are acceptably low.

Engineering synthesis: dependable supply is an additional unsolved capability, beyond the performance of an individual graft. Suitable hearts would need to be produced consistently, screened adequately and delivered when needed, with feasible resource requirements. The supplied review identifies organ expansion as an intended goal but provides no demonstration of repeatable production capacity, delivery reliability or practical scale.

current_state.text: Griffith and colleagues’ Nature Medicine report, published on 8 January 2025, describes the reported second transplantation of a genetically modified pig heart into a living person: a 10-gene-edited heart was transplanted into a 58-year-old man with advanced heart failure. The available abstract reports excellent systolic and diastolic function during the first several weeks, followed by diastolic failure and near-complete loss of systolic function. Extracorporeal membrane oxygenation was instituted on postoperative day 31, and the patient transitioned to comfort care after 40 days. An available extended-data caption identifies an autopsy specimen at postoperative day 40, supporting the reported death at that time. This establishes initial human graft function followed by severe failure, without demonstrating durable replacement.

Access limits matter when interpreting that report. According to the supplied review, the retained article is a subscription preview containing the abstract and extended-data material, rather than the full main text. One supplement yielded very little extractable text, and the blot images in another were not inspected. The clinical account above rests on the reviewed abstract and caption; the supplements do not provide additional clinical confirmation in this record. These limitations constrain interpretation without showing that the reported findings are false.

On 15 May 2026, United Therapeutics announced FDA clearance under its Investigational New Drug application to proceed with EXPRESS, a clinical study of its investigational UHeart derived from a pig with 10 gene edits. The sponsor describes six added human genes intended to improve immunological acceptance and compatibility. The announcement establishes that the sponsor reported permission to conduct the study; it supplies no clinical outcome results and does not establish effectiveness. No independent FDA document is included in the supplied evidence.

The announced study selects patients without remaining therapeutic options and includes assessments of function, quality of life, exercise capacity and safety. After a 24-week post-transplant follow-up period, recipients are to be followed for life, including for patient survival, graft survival and zoonotic infections. Possible expansion to additional centers is described as a study plan. These provisions show what investigators intend to evaluate; they do not establish enrollment, completed follow-up, multicenter reproducibility or successful outcomes.

Evidence-scope synthesis: the supplied freshness record is empty, so these dated reports do not establish the latest clinical or regulatory position as of 1 November 2026, the review’s stated reference date. The review identifies the additional sponsor PDFs as unrelated to a relevant clinical update, including documents published after that date. Their presence in the source index does not resolve whether later transplantation results, trial milestones or safety findings occurred.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed clinical demonstration: a prospective multicenter program should show reproducible patient and graft survival over years, with sustained cardiac function, functional recovery and meaningful quality of life. Comparisons with appropriate human-heart transplantation benchmarks should account for recipient selection and baseline risk, particularly because the announced study targets patients without remaining therapeutic options. These are proposed criteria for a convincing breakthrough, extending the announced clinical goals; they are not established consensus thresholds or results already obtained.
completion_criteria.label: Reproducible multiyear patient and graft survival with functional recovery

completion_criteria.text: Proposed safety demonstration: longitudinal follow-up should characterize rejection, immunosuppression harms, arrhythmias, thromboembolic and ischemic events, opportunistic infections and possible animal-to-human pathogen transmission. The announced lifelong surveillance provides a basis for this requirement. Convincing evidence would need to show how these risks are managed alongside graft benefit, rather than relying on graft survival alone.
completion_criteria.label: Longitudinal safety risks characterized and managed alongside graft benefit

completion_criteria.text: Proposed supply demonstration: the same program should demonstrate a dependable, practical supply of suitably screened donor hearts through reproducible production, consistent organ quality, timely delivery and feasible resource requirements. Supply performance should be assessed across repeated transplants and participating centers. This addition is essential because clinical success with a small number of specially prepared organs would leave the concept’s defining supply claim unresolved.
completion_criteria.label: Dependable screened heart supply demonstrated across transplants and centers

completion_criteria.text: Proposed practical boundaries: demonstrations should specify the recipient populations, donor configurations, treatment regimens, center capabilities and follow-up duration to which the results apply. Repetition across patients, production batches and centers would establish demonstrated breadth under those conditions. Finite studies could not establish compatibility for every patient or exclude every rare or delayed harm, and no numerical pass threshold is established by the supplied material.
completion_criteria.label: Demonstrated breadth and applicability limits specified for transplant results

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: CAR-03, “A durable, broadly affordable total artificial heart,” shares the objective of replacing a failing heart but uses a mechanical device. CAR-07, “Produce a transplantable, fully engineered living human heart,” also seeks a new source of replacement organs, using engineered human tissue. CAR-04 instead depends on animal donor hearts and cross-species compatibility. These are distinct routes to cardiac replacement with different production and recipient-management requirements.

Roster-based synthesis: CAR-01, “Regenerate a severely damaged adult human heart,” aims to repair the recipient’s existing heart. CAR-05, “Correct inherited heart disease directly and durably in the beating heart,” and CAR-08, “Durably reverse heart failure with preserved ejection fraction,” likewise target disease within the existing heart. Success in those concepts could reduce the need for replacement in some patients, while CAR-04 addresses a supply of replacement organs. None establishes the others’ capabilities.

Roster-based synthesis: CAR-02, “Reliably reverse advanced atherosclerosis throughout the arterial tree,” and CAR-12, “Detect actionable coronary plaque risk before a first clinical event,” address arterial disease and prevention. CAR-06, “Make most preventable sudden cardiac deaths predictable and preventable,” CAR-09, “A durable, non-ablative cure for atrial fibrillation,” CAR-10, “Reverse established calcific aortic stenosis without valve replacement,” CAR-11, “Reverse pulmonary arterial hypertension and its cardiovascular consequences,” and CAR-13, “Broadly prevent cardiac injury from cancer treatment without weakening cancer control,” target distinct risks or diseases. They overlap with CAR-04 through preserving cardiovascular health or potentially reducing progression to severe disease, but transplantable animal hearts would not demonstrate any of those preventive or disease-reversal capabilities.

change_log.change: Defined the concept around both durable human cardiac replacement and a dependable donor-heart supply.
change_log.reason: The innovation’s identity requires repeatable clinical performance and practical supply; a single transplantation demonstrates neither in full.

change_log.change: Expanded the clinical account with the publication date, recipient age, 10-gene-edited graft, initial systolic and diastolic function, subsequent failure and ECMO on day 31.
change_log.reason: The supplied review supports these details and they clarify the demonstrated achievement and its limits.

change_log.change: Preserved the reported 40-day mortality while explaining its support in the abstract and autopsy caption.
change_log.reason: The reviewed material supports the timing despite incomplete access to the article.

change_log.change: Distinguished the May 2026 sponsor announcement, investigational clearance and planned follow-up from demonstrated trial outcomes.
change_log.reason: Permission to study the approach does not establish effectiveness, enrollment or completed follow-up.

change_log.change: Integrated rejection, coagulation, physiological compatibility, growth and infectious-safety barriers without assigning unsupported mechanisms or causal weights.
change_log.reason: The evidence supports these risk categories but does not establish their precise mechanisms or relative importance.

change_log.change: Added explicit proposed supply criteria and risk-adjusted interpretation of human-transplant benchmarks.
change_log.reason: The original completion criteria omitted the defining supply capability, and the announced recipient population complicates unadjusted comparisons.

change_log.change: Preserved partial article access, supplement extraction limits and the unresolved freshness of the evidence.
change_log.reason: These limitations affect interpretation and prevent the dated reports from establishing the latest status.

change_log.change: Explained conditional impact and relationships across the supplied concept roster.
change_log.reason: The record needs to distinguish cardiac replacement from repair and prevention, and avoid implying that heart xenotransplantation validates other organ programs.

unresolved_issues: Later clinical, trial or regulatory developments before 1 November 2026 remain unresolved because the supplied freshness record is empty.
The full Nature Medicine article was unavailable in the reviewed material; poorly extracted supplementary content and uninspected blot images cannot support additional findings here.
No independent FDA document accompanies the sponsor’s announcement of investigational clearance.
The supplied evidence does not establish years-long compatibility, acceptable long-term treatment harms or dependable production and delivery at practical scale.

Appropriate risk-adjusted comparators, acceptable outcome thresholds and feasible supply-resource requirements remain to be specified; the proposed completion criteria are not a published consensus standard.
The precise mechanisms and relative importance of rejection, coagulation and physiological differences in graft failure remain unresolved in the supplied material.
